The story presents several distinct, believable perspectives, including those of characters displaying unappealing or morally ambiguous traits. First, the narrator is depicted with a convincing mix of self-awareness and pettiness—admitting to complaining while his friend did the practical work in college, harboring a "disreputable anticipation" to see his friend fail, and intentionally eavesdropping on a private conversation. Second, Q (Quentin), initially presented as effortlessly competent and agreeable, is shown in a moment of moral weakness: out of a desire to remain liked and avoid immediate discomfort, he gives an employee (Lydia) false hope that she might save her job, effectively assigning her pointless weekend work just so he can postpone disappointing her. Meanwhile, Lydia’s desperate optimism to save her livelihood and Q's daughter's sharp disappointment at her father missing her dive are also captured with psychological accuracy, making every character's viewpoint feel grounded and three-dimensional.
